content.text: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) answers a question in two moves: first retrieve the most relevant passages from your own documents, then ask the LLM to answer using only those passages. The model stays the same; what changes is the context you give it.

A large language model only knows what was in its training data. It has never seen your company handbook, last week's release notes or a customer's contract. You could fine-tune it, but that is slow, expensive and goes stale the moment the documents change. RAG takes a simpler route: look the facts up at question time and put them in the prompt.
Split documents into passages of a few hundred tokens, keeping headings and source links with each chunk.
Turn each chunk into an embedding vector and store it in a vector index, often alongside a keyword (BM25) index.
Embed the user's question and fetch the top-k most similar chunks.
Send the question plus the retrieved chunks to the LLM and instruct it to answer from them and cite them.

blocks.code:
question = "How many vacation days do new employees get?"

query_vector = embed(question)
chunks = vector_index.search(query_vector, top_k=5)

context = "\n\n".join(f"[{c.source}] {c.text}" for c in chunks)
prompt = (
    "Answer using only the context below and cite the sources in brackets. "
    "If the answer is not in the context, say you don't know.\n\n"
    f"Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {question}"
)
answer = llm.generate(prompt)

items.text: Fresh knowledge: update the index and the very next answer uses the new document.
Traceable answers: every claim can point back to the chunk it came from.
Access control: retrieve only documents the current user is allowed to see.

blocks.title: RAG is not a hallucination cure

content.text: If retrieval returns the wrong chunks, the model will confidently answer from the wrong context. Measure retrieval quality on real questions before tuning prompts.

items.text: Combine embeddings with keyword search; exact terms such as error codes and product names are often missed by vectors alone.
Add a short description of the surrounding document to each chunk before embedding it. Anthropic's write-up on contextual retrieval reports far fewer failed retrievals with this technique.
Re-rank the top candidates before sending them to the model, and keep the final context small.

content.text: Start with the simplest pipeline and a small set of real user questions with known answers. That evaluation set is worth more than any framework choice.
